34.0.0.en: The Baals: that is, the altars of Baal, a well-known pagan god.

34.0.1.en: The images (poles): plural of a pole, a wooden pillar set up for the worship of foreign gods, whom they believed to be in heaven.

34.0.2.en: The molten images: the statues they cast for the pagan gods, that is, the idols they made from various metals.

34.0.3.en: Josiah reigned eight years, and when he was still a youth, after eight years, that is, when he reached the age of sixteen, and he was sixteen years old, his concern for the worship of God appeared, and he attached himself to Him with all his heart. Then twelve years after he ascended the throne, when he was twenty years old, he began his reforms. He first took care to remove the traces of idol worship from Jerusalem and all Judah, whether the idols, or the poles they had made for the worship of foreign gods, as well as the altars of the Baals that had been built on the high places for the worship of idols. So he destroyed everything connected with the foreign gods, such as the images of the sun that had been made for the worship of the sun, and he even beat them to pieces, then strewed them on the graves of the wicked who had worshipped these idols.

34.0.4.en: We notice here Josiah's early concern for the worship of God and for removing idol worship, from the time he was sixteen years old. Perhaps he benefited from the mistakes of his father and his grandfather, for his father Amon died young without repenting of his sins, and he died at the age of twenty-four, whereas his grandfather Manasseh repented in the last days of his life, when he was nearly sixty years old.

34.1.0.en: Josiah wanted to defile the pagan altars, so he burned the bones of the priests of the idols on them, so that no one could use them or their fragments. In this way he cleansed Jerusalem of every trace of idol worship. He was the first king to remove the altars from the high places, for the righteous kings who preceded him, from Solomon to Josiah, did not remove the pagan altars on the high places but made them for the Lord; yet the wicked kings returned and offered sacrifices to the idols on them. Therefore Josiah took care to remove and defile these altars on the high places, so that no traces would remain to help the wicked to worship on the high places. Although the kings who came after Josiah, that is, his sons, returned and worshipped idols and turned away from God. Thus the prophecy of the man of God was fulfilled, which he had spoken about three hundred years earlier, in the days of Jeroboam, the first king of Israel, that a king named Josiah would come and break down the pagan altars (1 Kgs 13:2). The people, who were immersed in the worship of idols, had forgotten the prophecies of God, but the word of God does not pass away.

34.2.0.en: Josiah was not content to cleanse his kingdom, that is, Jerusalem and Judah, but moved to remove idol worship in the other tribes, such as Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon and Naphtali, and even all the ruins around the cities in which idol worship had been established. These tribes were no longer an independent kingdom, for the kingdom of Assyria had taken possession of them, so Josiah seized this opportunity and boldly advanced to cleanse his brethren in the rest of the tribes of their attachment to idols, in order to bring them back to the worship of the Lord. This shows the extent of his zeal for the Lord and his love for all the Jews; even those who had gone astray and turned away for a time from the worship of God, Josiah tried to bring back, so that they might be one people who believe in God and reject the worship of idols.

34.2.1.en: He was meticulous in removing everything connected with idols, whether the altars, or the poles, or the statues such as the images of the sun, and he even beat them to pieces so that no part of them could be used afterward for evil worship. And after he completed the cleansing of the tribes that were called the kingdom of Israel, he returned with joy to his capital, the holy city of Jerusalem.

34.2.2.en: Be meticulous in removing every trace of sin from your house, and also leave behind every evil thought and everything that could bring you back to evil. When God sees your care, He will remove your sins from you and let you enjoy fellowship with Him.

35.0.s.en: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

35.0.0.en: The author of the book announces that Josiah kept the Passover at its appointed time, the fourteenth day of the first month, and that this was in the eighteenth year of his reign, that is, when he was twenty-six years old. Josiah was able to keep the Passover at its appointed time because he had found the book of the Law and prepared for keeping the Passover, whereas King Hezekiah was not able to keep the Passover at its appointed time, so he kept it a month late. Therefore Josiah's Passover is considered greater, because he kept it with full preparation for it.

35.0.1.en: Josiah's concern for the Passover is considered a great work, because the Passover is the most important of the feasts of the Jews. Their life began with it when they went out of the land of Egypt and were freed from its bondage, and it is also the end of the Jewish feasts, since Christ kept the Passover for the last time on Holy Thursday, and after it He instituted the Lord's Supper, which is the sacrament of the Eucharist, to which the Passover pointed.

35.0.2.en: How good it is to prepare for every spiritual practice, so that you may feel it and enjoy God. Pray psalms as you go to church and pray at its door, so that you may feel the Divine Liturgy, and prepare yourself for prayer with a reading, or a prostration (metanoia), or a hymn, to help you concentrate on the words of the prayer. God rejoices in your care, and gives you comforts and warm feelings.

35.1.0.en: Their charges: their duties and responsibilities.

35.1.1.en: After Josiah restored the Temple, which had been neglected, he took care to encourage the priests, and distributed the work among them according to their responsibilities, each one in his place, whether in the service of offering the sacrifices on the bronze altar, or the laver, that is, the sea for washing, or the service of offering incense, or the lampstand, or the showbread, in addition to their examining the people who came forward to worship, so that they would be clean and free of leprosy. This was according to what he had learned from the Law of Moses and from all those who taught him, as will appear in the following verses; that is, he was meticulous and careful about everything he had received, so that he might do everything in a way that pleases God.

35.2.0.en: Josiah took care to establish the Levites in their work, meaning by them the priests and the Levites, because the priests are part of the tribe of Levi. He describes them here by two things, to stress to them their commitment to both:

35.2.1.en: 1- Teaching the people the Law of God.

35.2.2.en: 2- Taking care to sanctify themselves, so as to be an example to the people.

35.2.3.en: He also commanded the priests to return the ark of the covenant of God to its place in the Holy of Holies, since it had been removed from its place for one of these reasons:

35.2.4.en: 1- Perhaps the wicked kings had removed the ark and put it in a side chamber in the Temple, because of their lack of concern for the worship of the Lord.

35.2.5.en: 2- Perhaps the righteous priests in the days of the wicked kings had hidden the ark in one of the chambers of the Temple, so that the hands of the kings would not reach it to break it up and use the gold that was on it.

35.2.6.en: Josiah commanded the Levites to take care of the service of the Lord in His house, to help the people in worship, and to guide them in all the rites.

35.3.0.en: Josiah asked the Levites to arrange, through their chiefs, the service that fell to them according to their fathers' houses, that is, to divide themselves into courses, each course serving the house of the Lord for a week, according to what David taught, and then his son Solomon, who divided the Levites into twenty-four courses, each course serving the house for a week twice a year. These courses were for the priests and also for the Levites (1 Chr 24). This shows Josiah's meticulousness and his concern to organize the service of the Temple in the fullest way.

35.4.0.en: Josiah commanded the Levites to keep the Passover at its appointed time, and he also asked them to sanctify themselves and to sanctify their brethren from the rest of the tribes, and to teach them how to choose the Passover lamb according to what the Law prescribed, to slaughter the lamb for them, and to teach them how to eat it. For Josiah had divided the courses of the Levites among the tribes, so that each group of Levites would be responsible for a number of their brethren, so that everything would be done with order and care in this great feast, the feast of the Passover, as the verse indicated in (v. 5): "according to the divisions of the families of the fathers of your brethren the people, and after the division of the family of the Levites."

35.4.1.en: We notice Josiah's command to the Levites to sanctify themselves and to sanctify their brethren in preparation for keeping the Passover. Purity and cleanness are a necessity in the life of any servant before he begins his service, so that he cleanses his heart by repentance and prayer.

35.5.0.en: So that the Passover might be completed and none of the people might excuse himself because of his poverty, Josiah gave from his own property thirty thousand lambs and kids for keeping the Passover. In addition to that, he also gave three thousand bullocks, for the people to make into peace offerings, that they might rejoice with the Lord in gladness at this great feast. The king also gave kids, which were acceptable for keeping the Passover and which the poor offered because their price was lower than that of lambs (Ex 12:5). This shows two things by which Josiah was distinguished:

35.5.2.en: 2- His great concern that all the people keep the Passover and rejoice with God with peace offerings.

35.6.0.en: The chief priests who were in the house of the Lord followed the king's example, Josiah, in his giving for the feast of the Passover, so they too gave a large gift: two thousand six hundred lambs for keeping the Passover and three hundred bullocks for peace offerings.

35.7.0.en: The chiefs of the Levites also followed King Josiah's example, so they gave five thousand lambs for the Passover and five hundred bullocks for peace offerings. This shows the submission of the servants, that is, the priests and the Levites, to the king, their following his example, and their fear of God; that is, holiness had spread through the whole kingdom, and this of course gladdened God. If you compare the gifts that King Josiah and his chiefs gave (vv. 7-9) with what Hezekiah and his chiefs gave (ch. 30:24), you will notice that Josiah and his chiefs were more generous than Hezekiah. This shows Josiah's great concern and the favorable circumstances that helped this giving more than Hezekiah's straitened financial circumstances. Consequently, this Passover was the greatest Passover kept throughout the era of the kings.

35.8.0.en: With this great organization, the priests, the Levites and the people were prepared to keep the Passover. The priests slaughtered the animals and the Levites flayed their skins, and the priests sprinkled the blood on the bronze altar. This was a new rite which had not been done in the days of Moses in Egypt, since Moses had not yet received the Law and the system of sacrifices in full.

35.9.0.en: The priests removed the portions set apart for the sacrifice, to be offered to God on the bronze altar and burned on it (Lev 3:9), and then they gave the rest of the sacrifice for the people to roast and eat. They would slaughter and remove what was offered for the burnt offering, and then distribute the rest to the people according to their fathers' houses; that is, everything was done with precise order despite the vastness of the work. The priests also did this with the peace offerings from the bullocks, as they did with the Passover sacrifices. All this was according to what the Law of Moses prescribed.

35.10.0.en: The cauldrons: plural of cauldron, a large pot.

35.10.1.en: The dishes: plural of dish, which is a plate.

35.10.2.en: After the priests slaughtered the Passover and the Levites flayed it and gave it to the people, the people took it and roasted it, as the Law prescribed, although in the Hebrew original the word "roasted" and the word "boiled" in this verse are a single word, "bashal," which means to cook; that is, they cooked it, as is mentioned in (Deut 16:7). After that they boiled the peace offerings, which are the holy things, in pots, and put them in dishes for them to eat. Perhaps the Levites helped in the cooking and then gave to the people.

35.11.0.en: After the Levites made sure that the Passover had been prepared for all the people, they took care to prepare the Passover for the priests, that is, they cooked it for them, because the priests were busy offering up the portions of the sacrifices that were to be burned for God on the bronze altar. Finally, the Levites prepared the Passover for themselves and ate it.

35.11.1.en: Here the Levites' care appears, first for the people and then for themselves at the end. This is true love: that a person put the other before himself and arrange the needs of others before his own needs.

35.12.0.en: He adds here also that courses of the Levites carried out other works during the feast of the Passover, such as:

35.12.1.en: 1- The singers, that is, the Levites responsible for praise, under the leadership of the sons of Asaph, who praised throughout the period of the celebration of the feast of the Passover, according to what David had done when he appointed the chiefs of the singers, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, and all those who followed them from among their brethren the singers. So Josiah took care to complete the same order of praise.

35.12.2.en: 2- The porters, who were responsible for guarding the gates of the Temple.

35.12.3.en: For all these courses, their brethren the Levites took care to prepare the Passover for them because of their being occupied with their service, so that in the end all might eat and rejoice together at the feast of the Passover.

35.12.4.en: From this appears Josiah's meticulousness in carrying out all the rites that had reached him, whether from the Law of Moses (vv. 6, 12, 13) or from his fathers David and Solomon (v. 4).

35.13.0.en: Thus Josiah completed the Passover and had everyone celebrate it, and then they celebrated the feast of unleavened bread after it, which lasted seven days. The Passover signifies the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, and the unleavened bread, which is free of leaven, signifies the pure life, far from evil, which is lived by the person who belongs to Christ and receives his salvation through the Church and her sacraments.

35.13.1.en: We notice the importance of the service of the Levites, which includes the greatest works and the least, yet all are important because they are offered to God faithfully. They carried the ark of the covenant of God, and they also took care of flaying the animals, cooking them and putting them in dishes.

35.14.0.en: This Passover which Josiah completed in the eighteenth year of his reign was the greatest Passover kept throughout the period of the kings. None like it had been kept since the days of the judges, the last of whom was the prophet Samuel. All the people of the kingdom of Judah took part in it, as well as their brethren from the tribes who had obeyed God and responded to Josiah's call.

35.14.1.en: It appears from what has preceded in this chapter and the one before it that Josiah took care to cleanse and remove the idols, then to restore the house of the Lord, and God favored him with the discovery of His commandments, and then he moved to renew his covenant with God by keeping the Passover. Whoever cares to repent of his sins and to build his spiritual life, God reveals to him His knowledge, and he renews his covenant with God. This is accomplished through repentance and confession, Communion from the Holy Mysteries, care to read God's commandments and keep them in the Holy Bible, and care for spiritual edification, that is, for all the means of grace.

35.15.0.en: Necho: the Pharaoh of Egypt, called Necho II, of the twenty-sixth dynasty, who reigned in the period (610-595 BC). Carchemish: a city on the north of the Euphrates River, lying east of Aleppo.

35.15.1.en: After Josiah kept the Passover in the eighteenth year of his reign (v. 19), thirteen years passed in quiet, since Josiah reigned thirty-one years (ch. 34:1). During them Josiah continued to hold fast to the worship of the Lord, but his people in the kingdom of Judah were not wholehearted before God. This means that Josiah was not able to remove completely the effects of the corruption done by King Manasseh and after him his son Amon from the hearts of the people. Although Josiah removed idol worship, the people continued to love it, and perhaps kept some statues in their houses, as is proved by the following:

35.15.2.en: 1- God did not allow the captivity in the days of Josiah because of his own humbling of himself and his returning to God.

35.15.3.en: 2- God's wrath against His people remained, as mentioned in the words of the prophetess Huldah (ch. 34:22-28).

35.15.4.en: 3- All the sons of Josiah walked in idol worship after him and the people were led by them; that is, their hearts were still attached to idols, and even the house of Josiah himself, that is, his sons, loved idols.

35.15.5.en: In the thirty-first year of Josiah's reign, when he was thirty-nine years old, he learned that Necho, king of Egypt, had moved with his army toward Carchemish, claiming that he would help Assyria against the strong countries around it, such as Media, Persia and Babylon. Josiah feared the return of strength to Assyria, because he had taken advantage of its weakness and had taken possession of some of the lands of the tribes that were subject to it, until he reached the plain of Jezreel and Samaria (2 Kgs 23:15-20). So he rose up to fight Necho and block him from reaching Carchemish. We notice here, in this situation, that despite Josiah's piety and his holding fast to the worship of God, he did not first ask God before this war, and this was a mistake that led to his death. Perhaps he did not ask God because of a spiritual coldness that came over him, though he continued to worship God, he and all his capital Jerusalem (2 Chr 34:33).

35.16.0.en: The valley of Megiddo: a plain beside Mount Tabor, lying on the main road between Egypt and Mesopotamia, that is, Iraq.

35.16.1.en: When Necho learned that Josiah had risen with his army to fight him, he sent to him to keep out of his way, and assured him that he did not wish to fight him and that God, the God of Pharaoh, to whom he had prayed, had not directed him to fight Josiah. Here we find a divine warning on the lips of this pagan man, Necho, to Josiah, so that he too might return to his God and ask Him whether he should fight Necho or not. For God wished to save Josiah to the last moment, but he rushed in to fight Necho and did not seek God. He drew up a battle plan and disguised himself as an ordinary soldier and did not wear his royal robes, perhaps thinking to protect himself by this, and forgetting that God alone protects His children. In this he fell into the same error as the wicked Ahab, who relied on his own mind alone and disguised himself, and was killed in the battle (2 Chr 18:29). This means that Necho's word to Josiah was a message from God to him, so that he might examine himself. There is also an opinion that the God of whom Necho spoke is the God of Israel, who perhaps appeared to Necho and encouraged him to fight Assyria; in this way, the meaning of Necho's word to Josiah would be that the God of Israel is the One who moved Necho against Assyria and not against Josiah.

35.17.0.en: God allowed King Josiah to be struck by an arrow in a dangerous place, so he was gravely wounded, perhaps the arrow struck him in his heart. So the king asked those with him to carry him to a second chariot, because he felt the seriousness of his condition, hoping that they might be able to treat him, or at least that they would not leave him in the hands of the enemies, lest they deal cruelly with him.

35.18.0.en: Josiah's servants quickly moved their king to his second chariot, which was traveling beside him, and hurried to take him out of the battle and returned with him to Jerusalem. There he died, and they buried him in the tombs of the kings with great honor. The people of Jerusalem and Judah gathered and wept for him and made a great mourning for him.

35.18.1.en: Thus Josiah died as God had told him through the prophetess Huldah, before he saw the ruin and destruction of Jerusalem and the land of Judah, because he was a devout man who humbled himself before God and kept His commandments (ch. 34:22-28).

35.19.0.en: All the great men took part in weeping for King Josiah, the righteous one, the like of whom had not arisen from the days of David nor afterward on the throne of Judah. The great prophet Jeremiah came forward and composed a lamentation for him (Jer 22:10, 11), and Jeremiah referred to him in his Lamentations (Lam 4:20). The singing men and singing women took part in lamenting Josiah, and for many years they continued to lament him, and they made it a necessity for all the singers to remember the great Josiah and lament him all the days. All this shows the extent of the people's love for him and their faith in his righteousness and piety.

35.19.1.en: The lamentations of Josiah were written in the book of lamentations, which is different from the book of the Lamentations of Jeremiah. Perhaps it was a book among the Jews in which they gathered the lamentations for great men.

35.20.0.en: The rest of the detailed events of Josiah's life, his love for his people, and his walking according to the law of the Lord from his childhood to the end of his life, all this was written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel and Judah, which is not one of the books of the Holy Bible, but a historical book.

35.20.1.en: Be careful all your life to seek God before every matter, small or great. Do not be content that you live in the Church and that you have sought God in some important matters of your life, but persevere in seeking God every day and before every work, however small it may seem.

35.20.2.en: Note: see the life of Josiah at the end of the book.

35.20.3.en: The last four kings of the kingdom of Judah
